PHSCS 587

Temperature and threshold

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how an illustrative local temperature coefficient shifts threshold voltage

Thermal voltage UT = kT/q increases with temperature. Intrinsic carrier concentration nᵢ(T) changes strongly as well. The body potential φF = UT ln[NA/nᵢ(T)] therefore cannot be evaluated by changing UT while holding every other temperature-dependent term fixed.

A local compact approximation is Vth(T) ≈ Vth(T₀) + αT(T − T₀), where αT has units V/K. Silicon MOS thresholds often fall with temperature over an ordinary operating range, but the coefficient depends on doping, flat-band voltage and the threshold definition.

Current does not follow threshold alone. Mobility, leakage, series resistance and the chosen operating region also change with temperature. A lower threshold and lower mobility can push current in opposite directions.

A hot-leakage specification poses a separate design question: how large must the nominal threshold be to keep Ioff below its limit at the highest operating temperature? That required design target can rise even while the actual threshold of a particular device falls as it warms. Evaluate the measured Vth(T), thermal voltage and leakage model together when testing the specification.

Example

For an explicitly assumed αT = −1.0 mV/K, warming from 300 K to 330 K shifts threshold by −30 mV. This is a local estimate using the supplied coefficient, not a value to apply to every MOSFET.

Sources and scope
  • PHSCS 587 reading: 5.3–5.4, temperature dependence of threshold
  • PHSCS 587, 6.3–6.3.3.1 recording 2: temperature, off-current specifications and threshold tradeoffs.

Practice

1. Why is a lower threshold insufficient to conclude that a heated MOSFET has higher on-current?

Identify a transport quantity that changes in the opposite direction.

Channel mobility commonly decreases as phonon scattering grows. The net current change depends on mobility, gate overdrive, bias region and other temperature-dependent effects.
